items.text: Auction Optimizer: record any nomination, at the price it actually sold for. An auction is driven by nominations, and the room nominates whoever it likes — so most of a real auction gets recorded from the searchable board rather than from the handful of names shortlisted for your roster. Every row on that board now has a price box beside its two buttons: search the player who was just put up, type what he went for, and record whether you won him or which team did. Leave the box empty and we record what he is worth at today's prices — the greyed-out number the box is already showing, so what you see is what gets written. It is the same box wherever a player appears, so a price typed in one place is the price recorded in the other. Prices are what drive everything else on the screen: a sale recorded at the wrong number moves the inflation multiplier, every team's remaining money and every max bid with it.

Auction Optimizer: a live tool for auction leagues, beside the snake Draft Optimizer. An auction is not a draft with prices attached — it hands every team a fixed budget, and what your money is worth changes every time somebody else spends theirs, so it needs its own tool. Every player now carries a dollar value for your league size and budget: the room's money, minus the dollar every roster spot has to cost, shared out by how far each player is projected above the last startable player at his position. It is shown as a range rather than a single figure, because the range is the projection's own 80% interval priced in dollars — what he is worth if the season goes well or badly, not a guess at what he will go for. As players sell you record the price, and the board re-prices itself: if the room has overpaid there is less money left chasing the same players, so everyone remaining gets cheaper, and the tool says so in a single multiplier. Your max bid on anyone is the smaller of what he is worth at today's prices and the most you can pay while still leaving a dollar for every slot you have left to fill — so it will never walk you into an empty starting spot with no money to fill it. Each bid says which of those two numbers it came from. There is also a nomination panel: put up players you want when prices are soft, and expensive players you do not want when you are the one with money to spare. We do not model what your room will actually pay for anyone, so a value is what a player is worth, never a prediction of his price.

Draft recommendations: a tight end no longer wins your FLEX seat unless he actually out-projects the running backs and receivers beside him. Value over replacement compares a player to the last startable player at HIS OWN position, which is exactly right for a slot only he can fill — and the wrong yardstick for a FLEX, which does not care which position walks into it. On this year's board, replacement level sits about 19 points lower at tight end than at running back or receiver, so every tight end carried that much of a head start into a comparison he does not deliver in your lineup. A FLEX-only candidate is now measured against what could actually replace him in that seat, which makes the comparison a comparison of projected points. Measured over 200 simulated drafts on the served board, it changes the top recommendation on 3 to 6 percent of picks, all of them in rounds three through seven, and in every single case the pick it replaces is a tight end at FLEX. Your dedicated tight end starter is untouched — taking the best one before the cliff is still the advice there. This is the shared engine, so the live Draft Optimizer changes with it.

Mock draft: after the draft you can open every team's starting lineup, ranked by projected starter points, so you can see what the room actually built and judge for yourself whether it drafted like a draft room. Player names on the results screen and the roster panel open their player page in a new tab, and your roster now shows each player's bye week — amber when another player at the same position shares it, which is the clash that costs you a lineup slot.

Draft screens: a longer recommendation reason was widening the whole page, giving it a horizontal scrollbar and pushing the roster panel off the right edge. Fixed on both the mock draft and the live Draft Optimizer, and the reason itself is shorter now — it names the score and the player's published VOR, with the explanation moved into the panel's tooltip.

Mock draft: the two post-draft value lists were the wrong way round. "Fell furthest past ADP" was showing the players you reached for and "Taken earliest vs ADP" the ones who fell to you. Both now read as labelled, and the ADP column shows the player's own average draft position rather than his rank within it.

The NFL menu is grouped by what you are trying to do — Rankings & research, Draft, My leagues — rather than one list of twelve. Mock Draft now sits directly beside the Draft Optimizer, which is the pairing it should always have had.

Mock Draft: practise a full draft against CPU opponents, any time of year. Pick your format, league size and draft slot, and the room drafts around you — each seat with its own habits, blending market ADP with our projections, so players we like and the market does not actually fall to you. You draft with the same recommendations and the same reasoning the live Draft Optimizer gives you, then see how your roster came out: projected starter points against the rest of the room, position by position, and which of your picks fell furthest past ADP. Quick eight-round or full-roster, and a Skip button when you do not want to wait on the clock.

The mock draft's results screen says plainly what it is measuring. It ranks the room on our own projections — the same numbers the recommendations use — while the CPU teams draft partly off market ADP, so following the board closely is most of what a high finish there means. That is on the screen beside the rank, not buried in a tooltip.

The draft board is rebuilding daily again. Since 16 August the automated rebuild had been unable to read the kicker and defence projections, and rather than publish a board missing two positions it published nothing — so the board you were reading was correct, but it had stopped picking up new market and depth-chart data. It is advancing again, and the check that stopped the bad board from shipping is unchanged.

Kickers and defences are back on the draft board. A board rebuild on 16 August published without them, so every rostered K and D/ST on My Teams showed no projection at all. They are projected again, and the board now refuses to publish if a whole position is missing rather than shipping a board with a gap in it.

When a player on your roster has no projection beside him, My Teams now says why: a position we have not published, a name we could not match, or a position we do not project at all. Those are three different things with three different answers — and only one of them is fixed by re-importing your league, which the page now tells you.

My Teams reads properly on a phone. The roster and summary tables had a fixed minimum width, so you had to drag them left and right to reach the points column — on the one page most likely to be opened on a phone. The tables now fit the screen, dropping the two least important columns on a narrow one so the projection and the bench figure are always in view.

My Teams now shows what each of your teams is projected to score — twice. "Your current starters" totals the lineup your platform reports; "your best possible lineup" totals the best legal one we could field from the same roster. The difference is the headline: how many projected points you are leaving on your bench, league by league. Both figures are full-season projections before kickoff, scored on that league's own rules, so the bench number is unaffected by the differences between your leagues. A summary at the top orders your teams by their best possible lineup — a rough guide only, since your leagues neither score the same way nor start the same number of players, and the page says so beside the table.

Memberships are open. The first 100 members pay $10/month, locked in for as long as the membership stays active; after that it is $20. Cancel any time from Settings — access runs to the end of the period you have already paid for, and the page tells you the exact date.

On a phone, the Props filters now sit behind a "Filters" button, closed by default, with a count of how many you have set. A full slate carries all 30 clubs, so that panel had grown to about twenty lines you scrolled past before reaching a single game. Desktop is unchanged.

The player dropdown in "Log a prop" was empty for everyone, on every date — two stacked failures in the reads behind it, both fixed. Those reads now report why they failed instead of returning an empty list, which had looked exactly like a day with nothing scheduled yet.

Total Bases now has the same one-click "Log this prop" button as the strikeout pages. It copies the batter, the book you pick and its posted line into your Bet Log, where it settles against the batter’s real total bases once the game is final.

You can now log a batter total-bases prop to your Bet Log. "Log a prop" only understood pitcher strikeouts, so a total-bases bet you had actually placed could not be recorded. It now asks which prop type you are logging and offers every batter in that day’s posted lineups. Bookkeeping only — not betting advice.

NFL draft-board point totals now sit at the level players actually produce. Our track record showed expected points running below realized totals for the draftable tier, and the cause was the per-game rate. A per-position correction, fitted only on finished seasons, moves running backs up about a quarter, receivers and tight ends about a tenth, and quarterbacks down about seven percent. Order within a position and the 80% range are unchanged — this corrects the number toward what happened, it does not make us better at ranking players.

The draft board now rebuilds daily through draft season and reads the current market when it does. Average draft position and expert rankings had been coming from a cache nothing could refresh, so a board could be pricing against a market three weeks old — and those inputs feed the sort order, not just the ADP column. A fresher build is not a better model.

Every fantasy page now dates each input separately, not just the board build. One date used to stand for the projection, the ADP column beside it and the depth charts behind it — on the 10 August board that read 8/10 over a market snapshot from 25 July. Where we genuinely cannot tell how old an input is, it now says "unknown".

The Roster Report now has a League tab: every team in your league, filled by our optimizer and totalled on your league’s own scoring. It ranks projected starting points — not a projected finish, and not a chance of winning anything. We do not know what lineup another manager will start, so every team is filled the same way yours is, and rosters are as they stood when you imported.

Your league defence now scores. Your platform calls it "Lions D/ST" while our board calls it "DET D/ST", so no team defence ever matched by name — the D/ST slot sat empty and its points were missing from your projected team total. Defences are now matched by team.

The Roster Report’s wire section is now a real free-agent pool. We keep every team’s roster at import, so it lists players on nobody’s roster in your league rather than only players outside the pool a league your size drafts. It is the picture from when you imported — we never re-read your league.

The Props page has a Total Bases tab: our per-batter total-bases projection beside each sportsbook’s line. Each card opens a full distribution — the projected range, the chance of 1+, 2+, 3+ and 4+ bases, and our probability against each book’s de-vigged price. A projection and transparency comparison only, not betting advice.

The Props page is now organized by game rather than one long card grid — a full slate can be 100+ quoted batters. Games are collapsible sections in start-time order, plus a team filter, a name search and a Sportsbook filter. Sort still opens on slate order; you can instead order by projection, by our probability of 2+ bases, or by the gap to the book’s number — never a "top plays" pick.

Total Bases was missing entire games that Strikeouts still showed, including games already under way — a batter only appeared once a book had a currently-live line, so a game starting dropped every batter in it. It is now built from posted lineups, with a book line shown when one is available.

A Post-Draft Roster Report. Import your drafted league and one page reads your team back in your league’s own scoring: your starting lineup and its season projection with an 80% range, where you are strong and thin, what each bye week costs, the best names on the wire, and the trade shape your roster suggests. It will not grade your draft or predict where you finish, and it compares you to an average team with your settings rather than to the other managers in your league.

"Our rank" on the home page now means what it means on the rankings page. It had been our rank among the players the market actually drafts, while the rankings page ranks everyone we project — on the current board that is 23 tight ends against 169. The card now shows the full-board rank, so the number you read is the number you find when you click through.

Kickers and defenses no longer sit among the skill players in the board’s "Available players" list. Last week’s fix only covered the recommendations panel, so a defense you had just been steered away from reappeared near the top of best-available. Both surfaces now share one ordering rule. Their overall-rank number is blank rather than comparing them to skill players; position rank (DST4, K2) still sits beside the name.

The draft optimizer no longer suggests a kicker or defense in the early rounds — on the current board, round six came back five-sixths kickers and defenses. Their value over replacement is real but smaller than the noise around it, so they are now held back until your roster actually needs them.

The draft optimizer will no longer let you finish a draft with an empty starter slot. Recommendations could drift onto bench depth — a full 12-team test draft finished with both running-back spots empty. Once every remaining pick is needed to fill a slot, it only suggests players who fill one. The same draft now finishes nine of nine.

The draft optimizer’s recommendations had a ranking bug affecting every position: the scarcity bonus for a steep drop-off went to whoever sat directly above the cliff, regardless of how good he was. Across the board, 445 pairs ranked a worse player above a better one at the same position. The bonus now belongs to the position and goes to the best player still available there.
You can now sign in with just your email — we send a six-digit code, so there's no password to set or forget. Google sign-in still works as before.

A free account now includes one personalized league. Import it from Sleeper, Yahoo or ESPN — or enter your scoring by hand — and your board is re-scored for your actual settings, with value over replacement computed against your real starting lineup. My League leads with what changed in your scoring, and why.

The NFL fantasy rankings and projections are now free to read, with every number real — our projection, rank, 80% range and market ADP for every player, no account needed. The free board is full-PPR, twelve-team; other formats and league sizes are part of a membership.

Rankings and the League Board now show how far each player has moved from our generic board once you select your own league — the "vs our generic board" comparison that used to live only on My League.

A "full-season rate" column now sits beside expected points on the rankings, projections and player pages — what a player is worth in the weeks he plays, stretched over a full 17 games, so two players with different injury risk are easier to compare.

Our projected points are now labelled "Expected pts" everywhere. They already price in the games we expect a player to miss, so they run lower than an "if he plays every week" number — the Track Record shows projected games beside them so you can see the discount. Point rankings are unchanged.
The membership page now shows the price, billing period and remaining founding-member seats before you sign up — read straight from Stripe, so what's advertised is what's billed.
You can now create an account yourself — one click with Google, or with your email. Signing up is free, you subscribe when you want to, and you land back on whatever page you started from.
Player Search no longer requires an account, and a retired player's page now shows his past seasons instead of "player not found".
On a phone, the menu no longer runs off the bottom of the screen — Sign Out and Settings are always reachable, and it scrolls on its own without moving the page behind it.

My League now lets you switch between every saved league you have, instead of always showing whichever one happened to load first. If you've saved more than one league — a subscriber account can save several — a picker at the top of the page lists them by name; choosing a different one re-scores the whole page, board and all, for that league, and your choice sticks through a refresh. A free account only ever has one saved league, so nothing changes there.

A new My Teams page (NFL → Fantasy) shows every league you've imported in one place, each roster scored under that league's own format. Tell us which team is yours and your starters and bench show up with a season projection and 80% range. Per-game splits and waivers arrive with the weekly model.

Opened three NFL fantasy pages under NFL → Fantasy — Projections, Rankings and the League Board. Every player's 2026 projection is re-scored for your league's format and size, with an 80% range on every number and value over replacement on the board.

Kickers and defenses (K and D/ST) are now projected, and your league's exact scoring applies precisely — field goals by distance, the points-allowed tier table, and yards-allowed tiers — because we emit raw components rather than a single total. These are the least predictable positions, so read them as a streaming tier with wide ranges, not a precise rank.

Every player now has his own page — full projected stat line, fantasy points under standard, half-PPR, full-PPR and your own league, his 80% range drawn as a band, position rank, value over replacement, tier, and where the market is drafting him. Reach it from any board or from Player Search.

Player pages gained a headshot and bio, a breakdown of what pushes each player's number up or down (in actual points, from a separate research model — a second independent read, not a receipt for the projection), and a subscriber History panel: how he finished each season back to 2019, that year's ADP, a weekly injury log, and a plain-language consistency read.

Added market ADP to the Rankings and League Board, with a "vs ADP" column showing where our board and the public disagree — matched to your scoring format and league size. It's a reference point, not a claim our order is the better one.
The boards gained value tiers (a break where there's an unusually large drop to the next player), named replacement-level players, pagination, and clearer self-explaining column labels.

Players who sat out all of last season (Brandon Aiyuk, Tank Dell) are back on the board — projected off their most recent season played, with a hard availability discount and a Low-confidence badge, so they usually sit below where the market drafts them.

We recalibrated our 80% projection ranges against what players actually did. The old method under-covered badly — only ~55% of veterans finished inside their range — so ranges are now read from comparable players' real outcomes, position by position, and are honestly wider (a late-round veteran's floor is often zero). Point projections are unchanged.

Pick email alerts now arrive as lineups confirm through the day, when your lineup-confirmed picks are ready — instead of a single morning email built on preliminary picks. Moneyline and totals only, each pick emailed once.

Fixed a scoring bug where ESPN-imported leagues ignored passing, rushing and receiving yards — the bulk of fantasy scoring — so those boards had been ranking almost entirely on touchdowns and receptions. Every ESPN league is now corrected with no re-import needed. Sleeper and Yahoo were never affected.

Fixed player pages showing an IL badge on healthy, playing players — 62 of the 187 flagged as injured had already played since. Status now clears whenever a player appears in a game, and is checked daily against that exact contradiction.

The MLB prospect board now shows a traded prospect's current organization and puts him on the right AL/NL sheet — org comes from MLB's own data instead of FanGraphs' editorial board, which doesn't repoint a player when he's traded.
The Settings page now tells you the truth about a canceled subscription — the exact date your access continues through, instead of still showing "Active subscription".

Bets on late games at the end of a month no longer sit "Pending" forever. We now ask MLB directly for a final when our own records don't show one, and alert ourselves if any bet stays pending more than a day after first pitch.
Strikeout prop bets in the Bet Log now settle the same night the game ends, graded from MLB's official box score, instead of waiting a day for our pitch-tracking data to rebuild.

We briefly swapped the model behind our projected run totals on August 2nd and reverted it the same day — re-scoring both showed the original was better calibrated, so we put it back. Neither model's per-game uncertainty is where we want it yet; that's what we're working on. Totals bets remain paused, and this was never a betting claim.

Added a "Predictive distribution" section to the totals pick-detail page — the model's full calibrated view of how a game's scoring could land: the game-total distribution with the market line drawn on it, an 80% range, the probability of the over, and per-team and alternate-line ladders. It's a transparency view of the model's uncertainty, not a bet recommendation.

Added two-factor authentication (Settings → Two-Factor Authentication) — turn on an authenticator app and enter a 6-digit code alongside your password each sign-in. If you sign in with Google, 2FA is already handled by your Google account.
Added "Continue with Google" to the sign-in page — sign in in one tap instead of typing an email and password. Credence never sees your Google password.

Win rate, record and ROI now mean exactly the same thing everywhere — win rate excludes pushes, records count one call per market, and ROI is your result net of the book's cut. Rates from only a handful of bets carry a plain "small sample" caveat, and the number of bets behind a rate is shown beside it.

A Parlay Calculator is here (Betting → Parlay Calculator). Build a parlay from the day's slate and see our model's true combined probability next to the price the book implies, plus expected value per dollar and a plain verdict. Same-game legs are correlation-adjusted rather than naively multiplied. Most parlays are negative expected value once the vig is priced in, and this is built to show you that.

You can now log a strikeout prop into your Bet Log — copied from a pitcher's projection, or back-logged for one you already placed — and it settles automatically against his actual strikeouts once the game is final.

Bet alerts (Settings → Notifications) — opt in to be told by email or browser push when the model posts qualified plays for the day. Most days nothing fires. These are model outputs, not betting advice.
Completed games now show a "who called it" scorecard — which side the model favored on the moneyline and total, and whether the call was right, shown as plainly for a miss as for a hit.

A new Props page (Betting dropdown) shows every probable starter's projected strikeout total for the day, with the book's posted line and the model-minus-book gap, sorted highest first. Click any card for the full distribution and per-book breakdown.

Starting pitcher pages now show our projected strikeout total for their next start, next to the book's line, with a per-book de-vigged Over% comparison. Single-game strikeout totals are high-variance — treat it as context, not a play.

The Performance page now shows a Bankroll by Sportsbook breakdown — balance, net deposits, betting P&L and growth per book. Growth is return on deposited funds, kept distinct from ROI (return on stake).

Each pick's detail page now shows a Line Movement chart across all seven books — how the moneyline and total drifted from open to current, with a de-vigged Over% view for totals. A market-context view, not an edge claim.

Matchup heatmaps are live on pick and player pages — a strike-zone heatmap of where a batter does damage, overlaid with where the pitcher actually locates each pitch type, with pitch-type toggles and per-cell detail. A show-your-work matchup view; the zone signal tested null for predictive edge.

Line Shopping on the EV Tracker — model-positive plays ranked by edge, with the best available US price and the book offering it highlighted per play, plus Pinnacle's fair-value anchor. On each pick, the best-priced book is marked with a "BEST" badge.
Settings now has a Sportsbooks section — add each book you use, set its balance, and record deposits and withdrawals, so bankroll growth reflects only betting results, not cash movement.

Book Comparison now shows a model breakeven price per pick — the price at which the model's edge reaches zero — alongside Pinnacle's no-vig fair value, and each book's hold (vig), with the tightest book flagged (Pinnacle ~2%, US books 4–8%).

The models behind the picks are now leak-free. The old ones over-credited a bullpen metric that was partly computed from the game being predicted; the new ones remove that and are far leaner, so the displayed "why this pick" drivers now reflect what the model actually weighs. Picks and probabilities may shift.

Win probabilities are now calibrated to be honest about how close most MLB games are — numbers shown near 75–85% were really closer to a coin flip. When we say 55%, the home team wins about 55%. Treat every pick as a lean, not a lock.

A Book Comparison panel on every game-detail page — pick a book and see its moneyline and totals prices alongside the model's probability, the book's de-vigged market %, and expected value per dollar, with Pinnacle as the sharp low-vig anchor.
Pick pages now show a model conviction score and an 80% win-probability range for moneyline picks — a confidence signal, showing how wide the model's uncertainty is, not a recommendation to bet.

A Teams directory (/teams) — all 30 MLB teams by division with record, win %, and streak — plus team pages with ELO trend, platoon splits, recent form, upcoming schedule with probable starters, and key stats.
A Players directory (/players) — searchable batter and pitcher lists with core stats, each linking through to a full player profile.
Pick pages now show model reasoning — a plain-English narrative plus signed feature drivers grouped by category (starting pitcher, bullpen, team offense, park & weather).
Blog posts are now public at /blog, with the latest surfaced on the home page.
FAQ and Contact pages published, covering model methodology, platform mechanics and responsible use.
